title: Communicable Disease Terminology
body:
## What it is
Vocabulary that the exam uses to separate look-alike ideas. Learn the contrasts, not just the definitions.

## Must-know facts
- **Infection**: an organism lodges and multiplies in host tissue and causes signs, symptoms and an immune response.
- **Carrier**: harbors and can pass on the organism but shows no disease. Hard to find, so an important source of spread.
- **Communicable disease**: caused by an infectious agent or its toxins, passed directly or indirectly (through a vector or object) to a well person. **Contagious** means it spreads easily from person to person.
- **Contact**: any person or animal closely associated with an infected person or freshly soiled material.
- **Infectious disease** (in this handout): needs direct inoculation through broken skin or mucous membrane, not casual contact.
- **Host**: the person, animal or plant a parasite depends on. **Habitat**: where an organism normally lives. **Reservoir**: the species (animal or plant) in which the agent lives and multiplies so it can reach humans.
- **Disinfection**: destroying pathogens on inanimate objects by physical or chemical means.
  - **Concurrent**: done right after the client discharges infectious material, while the client is still a source.
  - **Terminal**: done when the client is no longer a source, e.g. after discharge, to ready the room.
- **Isolation**: separating a sick person during the period of communicability.
- **Quarantine**: limiting movement of *exposed but not necessarily sick* people or animals for the longest incubation period of that disease.

## How the exam asks about it
- Isolation = the sick person; quarantine = the exposed person. This pair is a favorite.
- Concurrent vs terminal: ask whether the client is still the source.

## Related topics
[[Chain of Infection and Modes of Transmission]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]], [[Epidemiologic Triangle and Patterns of Disease Occurrence]]

title: Epidemiologic Triangle and Patterns of Disease Occurrence
body:
## What it is
Epidemiology studies how often disease occurs, who gets it and why, then uses that knowledge to control health problems. It is the foundation of disease prevention.

## Uses of epidemiology
- Track the rise and fall of disease over time.
- Diagnose the health of a community.
- Evaluate health services so they can be improved.
- Estimate risk of disease or accident and the chance of avoiding it.
- Complete the clinical picture and natural history of chronic disease.

## Epidemiologic triangle
- **Host**: the organism that harbors and feeds the agent.
- **Agent**: the microbe's built-in ability to survive, multiply and cause disease.
- **Environment**: all external conditions that affect the organism: biological, social, physical.
- Disease results when the three are out of balance.

## Patterns of occurrence
- **Sporadic**: a few scattered, unrelated cases (the handout's example is rabies).
- **Endemic**: the usual number of cases is always present in a place. Philippine examples given: schistosomiasis (Leyte, Samar), filariasis (Sorsogon), malaria (Palawan).
- **Epidemic / outbreak**: an unusually large number of cases in a short time.
- **Pandemic**: epidemics of the same disease in several countries at once (HIV/AIDS, SARS in the handout).

## How the exam asks about it
- Constant, expected level in a place = endemic, even if the level is high.
- Sudden excess above expected = epidemic.

## Related topics
[[Epidemiology and Endemic Diseases]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Epidemiology and FHSIS]], [[Communicable Disease Terminology]]

## Check against your textbook
Rabies is given as sporadic; in the Philippines it is also treated as a recurring public-health problem, so confirm how your reference classifies it.

title: Chain of Infection and Modes of Transmission
body:
## What it is
Infection needs six linked steps. Breaking any one link stops spread.

## The six links
1. **Causative agent**: bacteria, spirochetes, viruses, rickettsiae, chlamydiae, fungi, protozoa, parasites.
2. **Reservoir**: where the organism survives and multiplies.
3. **Portal of exit**: respiratory tract, genitourinary tract, GI tract, skin and mucous membrane, placenta.
4. **Mode of transmission**: how it travels from exit to a new host.
5. **Portal of entry**: usually the same routes as the exit.
6. **Susceptible host**: good defenses mean no infection; weakened defenses allow disease.

## Modes of transmission
- **Contact** (the most common): direct is person to person; indirect is through a contaminated object.
- **Droplet**: large respiratory particles from cough, sneeze or talk; travel only about 3 feet.
- **Airborne**: tiny particles or dust carrying microbes stay suspended; can travel farther than 3 feet.
- **Vehicle**: contaminated food, water, blood or articles that carry the organism until ingested or inoculated.
- **Vector-borne**: fleas, flies, mosquitoes carry the microbe to another living host.

## Nursing priority
The handout calls the mode of transmission the **easiest link to break**. In practice that means hand hygiene, barrier precautions, safe water and food, and vector control.

## Related topics
[[Isolation Categories and Precautions]], [[Types of Immunity and Antigens]], [[Communicable Disease Terminology]]

title: Types of Immunity and Antigens
body:
## What it is
Immunity is classified by whether it is natural or artificial and whether the body makes the antibodies (active) or receives them (passive).

## Must-know facts
- **Natural active**: after recovering from the disease.
- **Natural passive**: antibodies from mother to baby across the placenta.
- **Artificial active**: after a vaccine or toxoid.
- **Artificial passive**: antitoxin, antiserum, convalescent serum or immunoglobulin given ready-made.
- Active immunity lasts longer; passive is immediate but short-lived.

## Vaccine antigens
- **Inactivated (killed)**: immunity does not last long; needs multiple doses and boosters.
- **Attenuated (live, weakened)**: usually a single dose and long-lasting immunity. Live vaccines are avoided in pregnancy and in weakened immunity (see [[Measles (Rubeola)]]).

## How the exam asks about it
A baby protected by maternal antibodies = natural passive. A child given TIG or immune globulin = artificial passive.

## Related topics
[[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Vaccine Principles and Nursing Responsibilities]], [[Chain of Infection and Modes of Transmission]]

title: Isolation Categories and Precautions
body:
## What it is
Isolation separates people with communicable disease from others to prevent direct or indirect spread. Choose the category by how the organism travels.

## Categories in the handout
- **Strict**: highly contagious or virulent infections (chickenpox is listed here).
- **Contact**: spread by close or direct contact.
- **Respiratory**: spread through the air over short distances.
- **TB isolation**: smear-positive TB or a chest X-ray strongly suggesting active TB.
- **Enteric**: infections spread through feces (cholera, typhoid, dysentery, amoebiasis).
- **Reverse / neutropenic (protective)**: an immunocompromised client is protected from the environment.

## Precaution tiers
- **Standard precautions**: first tier, for all clients. Combines universal precautions (protect staff from blood-borne pathogens through mucous membrane or non-intact skin) with body substance isolation. Applies to blood, body fluids, secretions, drainage (except sweat).
- **Transmission-based precautions**: second tier for highly contagious clients: **contact, droplet, airborne**.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Apply standard precautions to everyone.
2. Add the transmission-based layer that matches the organism.
3. Teach family and visitors.

## How the exam asks about it
Match disease to precaution: measles, TB, chickenpox = airborne; pertussis, influenza, mumps, diphtheria (respiratory) = droplet; scabies, pediculosis = contact; cholera, typhoid = enteric.

## Related topics
[[Chain of Infection and Modes of Transmission]], [[Communicable Disease Terminology]], [[Tuberculosis: Features and Diagnosis]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout uses older isolation categories; current practice uses standard plus contact, droplet and airborne only. Confirm which your school expects.

title: Chickenpox (Varicella)
body:
## What it is
Acute, highly infectious viral disease (varicella-zoster virus, human herpesvirus 3) with sudden mild fever and a rash that moves through stages: flat-raised spots for hours, **vesicles for 3-4 days**, then granular scabs.

## Must-know facts
- Spread by respiratory secretions, direct contact, contaminated linen and fomites, and airborne.
- Scabs are not infective. Vesicle fluid and secretions are.
- Incubation about 2-3 weeks. Infectious from **2 days before the rash until 5 days after the first crop of vesicles**.
- Diagnosis: virus from vesicle fluid in the first 3-4 days; antibodies appear about day 7.
- Everyone not previously infected is susceptible; adults get it more severely; one attack gives long immunity and second attacks are rare.
- **Congenital varicella** can cause limb hypoplasia and scarring, growth retardation, brain and eye problems.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Isolate (airborne and contact) to protect others: exposure risk comes first.
2. Keep the child home until the lesions have crusted (handout: about 1 week after the rash starts) and avoid susceptible people.
3. Concurrent disinfection of nose and throat discharge.
4. Comfort: discourage scratching, teach correct use of topical antipruritics.

## Prevention
Varicella vaccine; **VZIG within 10 days of exposure** for high-risk exposed people.

## How the exam asks about it
Rash in different stages at the same time, or a pregnant or immunosuppressed contact who needs protection.

## Related topics
[[Herpes Zoster (Shingles)]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]], [[Communicable Disease Terminology]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout does not mention avoiding aspirin in children with chickenpox (Reye syndrome risk); confirm in your textbook.

title: Herpes Zoster (Shingles)
body:
## What it is
Painful, one-sided, band-like inflammation of a nerve root (dorsal root ganglion) caused by **reactivation** of the same virus that causes chickenpox. Usually seen in adults.

## Must-know facts
- Communicable from a day before the rash until 5-6 days after the last crust.
- Spread by airborne, droplet and direct contact (a susceptible person can catch chickenpox, not shingles, from it).
- Incubation is unknown, thought to be 13-17 days.

## Assessment findings
- Fever and malaise first.
- Severe deep pain, itching, tingling or hypersensitivity, mainly on the trunk.
- Red, unilateral nodular lesions about up to 2 weeks later, becoming fluid- or pus-filled vesicles. Cranial nerve involvement possible.

## Complications
CNS infection, transverse or ascending myelitis, long-lasting nerve pain.

## Treatment and nursing care
- Antiviral (acyclovir), analgesics, anti-inflammatory drugs.
- Airborne and contact precautions; cold compress if vesicles rupture; no scratching; bed rest and hygiene.
- Check pain relief after each analgesic.

## Prevention
Varicella vaccination; avoid contact with people who have chickenpox.

## Related topics
[[Chickenpox (Varicella)]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout says diagnosis separates zoster from herpes simplex by "fluorescent light"; verify the test name.

title: Measles (Rubeola)
body:
## What it is
Acute, highly contagious viral illness (paramyxovirus) with fever, respiratory symptoms and a rash. Also called rubeola, morbilli, 7-day measles.

## Must-know facts
- Spread by droplet, direct contact, articles with secretions, and airborne.
- Incubation 1-2 weeks. Communicable from just before the prodrome until **4 days after the rash appears**.
- **Koplik spots** are the pathognomonic sign (they appear before the rash).

## Assessment findings by stage
- **Pre-eruptive**: fever, cough, conjunctivitis, coryza, photophobia, Stimson line (red line on lower conjunctiva).
- **Eruptive**: maculopapular rash, high fever, anorexia, irritability, very sore red throat.
- **Convalescent**: rash fades, fever drops, skin peels (desquamation), appetite returns.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airborne plus standard precautions, ideally a negative-pressure room.
2. Lower fever (tepid sponge bath), keep fluids up.
3. Eye care (photosensitivity: dim light), ear, oral and nasal hygiene, skin care.
4. Watch for complications.

## Complications
Bronchopneumonia, pneumonia, otitis media, nephritis, encephalitis.

## Prevention
Measles vaccine at **9 months** (single dose in the handout); MMR later. **Do not give to pregnant women** or people with active TB, leukemia, lymphoma or weak immunity (live vaccine).

## Related topics
[[German Measles (Rubella)]], [[Mumps]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout lists "penicillin", an antiviral (isoprenosine) and a laxative. Measles treatment is mainly supportive and vitamin A is usually given; the MMR ages (15 months, 11-12 years) differ from current national schedules.

title: German Measles (Rubella)
body:
## What it is
Mild viral illness (rubella virus), also called three-day measles. Its real danger is **teratogenic effect on a fetus**.

## Must-know facts
- Droplet spread; transplacental spread causes congenital rubella.
- Incubation 2-3 weeks.
- Prodrome: low fever, headache, malaise, mild coryza and conjunctivitis, plus **post-auricular, sub-occipital and posterior cervical lymph node swelling** about the 3rd-5th day.
- Eruptive: Forchheimer spots on the soft palate; rash after the adenopathy, lasts 1-5 days, **no pigmentation or peeling**. Adults may have joint pain or arthritis; young men may have testicular pain.

## Congenital rubella
Growth retardation, low birth weight, "blueberry muffin" purpuric skin; heart defects (patent ductus, atrial septal defect), eye defects (cataract, glaucoma), microcephaly, intellectual delay, deafness. Infection in pregnancy can end in miscarriage.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Protect pregnant women: teach women of child-bearing age to avoid exposure.
2. Comfort: acetaminophen for fever and joint pain; darken the room, irrigate eyes with warm saline.
3. Cold compress if lymph nodes stay swollen.
4. Report confirmed cases.

## Prevention
Live attenuated MMR vaccine; immune serum globulin about a week after exposure.

## How the exam asks about it
A pregnant client exposed to rubella, or the question of when to vaccinate (not during pregnancy).

## Related topics
[[Measles (Rubeola)]], [[Mumps]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]]

## Check against your textbook
Dose timing of immune globulin and the pregnancy-avoidance interval after vaccination are not given in the handout.

title: Leprosy (Hansen's Disease)
body:
## What it is
Chronic infection by *Mycobacterium leprae* that attacks skin and peripheral nerves. Spread by airborne droplets and prolonged skin-to-skin contact. Incubation ranges from months to many years.

## Types
- **Lepromatous (multibacillary)**: most serious; skin lesions contain many bacilli; lepromin test **negative**; slow nerve damage with loss of sensation; can harm respiratory tract, eyes and testes.
- **Tuberculoid (paucibacillary)**: nerves and nearby skin; lepromin **positive**; elevated macules with clear centers; bacilli rarely found.
- **Borderline (dimorphous)**: features of both.

## Assessment findings
- Early: pale or reddish skin patches, loss of sensation, less sweating and hair growth over the patch, thick painful nerves, weakness, red eye, nasal blockage, non-healing ulcers.
- Late: loss of eyebrows and lashes (madarosis), cannot close eyelids (lagophthalmos), clawed fingers and toes, contractures, collapsed nose bridge, gynecomastia.

## Diagnosis and treatment
- Slit-skin smear.
- **Multidrug therapy**: multibacillary = rifampicin, clofazimine, dapsone for about 12 months; paucibacillary = rifampicin and dapsone for 6-9 months.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Protect anesthetic skin: check water temperature before use, proper footwear, avoid injury or pressure.
2. Eye care: daily tear substitute, protect against corneal ulcer.
3. Emotional support, rehabilitation, nutritious diet.
4. Report all cases and suspects; BCG and health education for prevention.

## Related topics
[[BCG and Pentavalent Vaccine]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout calls lepromatous "not infectious" but also lists multibacillary as "infectious type"; the second is the accepted view. Hospital isolation is not generally needed once treated. The blood-test changes listed are unusual; verify.

title: Scabies
body:
## What it is
Highly transmissible skin infestation by the itch mite *Sarcoptes scabiei*, causing burrows, itching and scratch lesions that can become infected.

## Must-know facts
- Spread by skin-to-skin contact and contaminated fomites. The mite can burrow and lay eggs within 24 hours of contact.
- Communicable as long as the host is infested.

## Assessment findings
- **Intense itching, worse at night.**
- Burrows in finger webs, wrists, elbows. In infants, young children, elderly or immunocompromised: also face, neck, scalp, ears.
- Diagnosis: scraping a burrow and viewing under a low-power microscope.

## Treatment
Permethrin cream left on 8-12 hours, aqueous malathion lotion, benzyl benzoate, sulfur in petrolatum; ivermectin for resistant cases; emollients or topical steroid for itch.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Contact precautions; terminal disinfection.
2. Teach correct drug application.
3. Cut nails short to reduce skin breaks.
4. Dry-clean or boil clothing and bedding.
5. **Treat and check all household and close contacts**; reinforce hygiene; allow the client to voice feelings.

## Complications
Persistent itching, excoriation, secondary bacterial infection.

## Related topics
[[Pediculosis (Lice Infestation)]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]]

title: Pediculosis (Lice Infestation)
body:
## What it is
Infestation by lice on the scalp, body or pubic area. Incubation about 3-7 days. Spread by head-to-head contact, fomites and sexual contact.

## Types
- **Capitis**: head lice; nits behind ears and nape.
- **Corporis**: body lice; live in clothing seams.
- **Pubis**: pubic lice; attach at the base of pubic hair, may reach eyebrows, lashes, axillae.

## Assessment findings
Itching (most common), tickling feeling of movement. Wood's light or microscope to confirm.

## Treatment
- **Permethrin or pyrethrin** topical insecticide is the initial choice for head and pubic lice.
- Fine-tooth comb dipped in vinegar; ordinary shampoo.
- Oral ivermectin, levamisole or albendazole are options.
- Wash clothes and linens in hot water, iron or dry-clean; storing items about 30 days or dry heat of 60 C kills lice.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Contact precautions until treatment is complete.
2. Protect yourself: gloves, gown and head covering when applying treatment.
3. Re-inspect for lice and eggs after each treatment; teach family to inspect.
4. Cut nails to avoid scratch infection; watch for drug reactions (sensitivity, CNS toxicity).
5. Teach correct use of lotions and shampoos (lindane can be absorbed and cause CNS problems).

## Complications
Excoriation, secondary infection, crusted scaly scarred skin if untreated.

## Related topics
[[Scabies]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]]

## Check against your textbook
Lindane is no longer preferred in many places because of neurotoxicity; confirm current first-line drugs.

title: Diphtheria
body:
## What it is
Acute infection of tonsils, throat, nose, larynx or wounds by *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* (Klebs-Loeffler bacillus). Marked by a **grayish pseudomembrane**. Humans are the reservoir.

## Must-know facts
- Spread by contact with a patient, carrier or soiled articles; milk can be a vehicle.
- Incubation 2-5 days. Communicable 2 weeks to over 4 weeks, until bacilli are gone from secretions and lesions.
- Types: nasal (foul serosanguinous discharge), tonsillar (lower fatality), nasopharyngeal (swollen cervical nodes, edematous neck), **laryngeal** (ages 2-5, the most severe and fatal; hoarseness progressing to loss of voice), cutaneous/wound.

## Assessment findings
Bull neck, gray pseudomembrane, sore throat, hoarse voice, breathing difficulty, low fever, malaise.

## Diagnosis
Nose and throat swab. **Schick test** (intradermal toxin; a positive reaction means no antibodies = susceptible). Moloney test detects sensitivity to toxoid.

## Priority nursing actions
1. **Airway first**: watch for obstruction and shock (collapse, anaphylaxis).
2. Absolute bed rest (about 2 weeks) to protect the heart.
3. Give antitoxin with correct technique; penicillin or erythromycin as ordered.
4. Soft diet, small frequent feeds; ice collar for neck.
5. Teach disposal of nasopharyngeal secretions. Peripheral neuritis may appear 2-3 months later.

## Prevention
Three doses of DPT in infancy, pasteurized milk, parent education, report cases.

## Related topics
[[Pertussis (Whooping Cough)]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]]

## Check against your textbook
Antitoxin requires a sensitivity test first; the handout does not state this. Schedule is now pentavalent in the EPI.

title: Pertussis (Whooping Cough)
body:
## What it is
Respiratory infection by *Bordetella pertussis* with repeated spasms of coughing that end in a crowing "whoop" and often vomiting.

## Must-know facts
- Spread by respiratory and salivary contact from laryngeal and bronchial secretions.
- Incubation 7-10 days (up to 3 weeks). Communicable from about 7 days after exposure to 3 weeks after typical paroxysms.

## Assessment findings
Violent coughing, nosebleed, distended neck veins, periorbital edema, conjunctival hemorrhage.

## Complications
**Bronchopneumonia (most dangerous)**, convulsions, umbilical hernia, otitis media, malnutrition from vomiting.

## Diagnosis
Nasopharyngeal swab, sputum culture, CBC (high white cells), chest X-ray (infiltrates, atelectasis).

## Treatment
Erythromycin or ampicillin; oxygen, fluids and electrolytes, nutrition. Post-exposure hyperimmune serum or gamma globulin.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway: suction at bedside, oxygen; watch breathing during paroxysms.
2. Isolation and medical asepsis (droplet).
3. Monitor intake and output because vomiting causes dehydration.
4. Small feedings after coughing spells, warm baths, keep bed dry.
5. Teach cough etiquette and handwashing.

## Prevention
Report every case; isolate patient 4-6 weeks per the handout; immunize with DPT and give boosters.

## Related topics
[[Diphtheria]], [[Tetanus (Lockjaw) Disease]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's isolation duration (4-6 weeks) is much longer than current practice (about 5 days of effective antibiotics).

title: Influenza
body:
## What it is
Acute viral respiratory infection (influenza virus A, B or C), also called la grippe.

## Must-know facts
- Droplet, direct contact and fomites.
- Incubation 1-3 days (up to 5). Infectious from 1 day before symptoms to 3-5 days after in adults.

## Assessment findings
Chills, very high fever, severe aches (especially back) with sweating, vomiting, sore throat, coryza and cough.

## Complications
Hemorrhagic pneumonia, encephalitis, myocarditis, sudden infant death syndrome, myoglobinuria.

## Diagnosis
Viral culture of throat wash in the first days, serology (complement fixation), leukopenia on blood count, chest X-ray, and ABG if severe.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Contact and droplet precautions.
2. Rest at home, lots of fluids, fever control (paracetamol, ibuprofen as ordered).
3. Watch for pneumonia: crackles, fresh fever, purulent or bloody sputum.
4. Teach tissue disposal, handwashing, avoid contact with others for at least 24 hours after fever is gone.

## Prevention
Yearly influenza vaccine; avoid crowds; do not share towels, glasses or utensils; public education on coughing and spitting.

## Related topics
[[Bird Flu (Avian Influenza)]], [[Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS)]], [[Pneumonia]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout says to avoid contact for "at least 24 hours"; confirm the exact period (usually 24 hours fever-free).

title: Anthrax
body:
## What it is
Bacterial disease from *Bacillus anthracis*, mostly of the skin but sometimes lungs, mediastinum or intestine. Called wool-sorter's or ragpicker's disease.

## Must-know facts
- Skin infection comes from contact with dying animals' tissue, contaminated wool or hair products, or soil and bone meal.
- Incubation usually 1-7 days (inhalation usually within 48 hours).

## Forms
- **Cutaneous** (over 90%): a pimple becomes an ulcer with a **black scab** ringed by purple vesicles; fatal in about 20% untreated.
- **Inhalational** (most fatal): flu-like onset, dyspnea, cyanosis, shock, death in 2-6 days; widened mediastinum on chest X-ray.
- **Intestinal**: eating infected meat; vomiting, bloody stool, septicemia; poor prognosis.

## Diagnosis
PCR is definitive; swabs of lesion, blood cultures, aspirates.

## Treatment
Antibiotics (ciprofloxacin is the drug of choice in the handout; also penicillin, doxycycline). Cutaneous: 7-10 days oral.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Collect cultures **before** antibiotics.
2. Supportive care by type; respiratory support in inhalational anthrax.
3. Teach: finish antibiotics, do not scratch lesions, wash with soap and water (alcohol rubs do not kill spores).
4. Anyone exposed must see a doctor immediately.

## Prevention
Treat animal products, supervise disposal of dead animals, vaccinate animals, protect workers.

## Related topics
[[Botulism]], [[Leptospirosis]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]]

## Check against your textbook
Anthrax duration for GI and inhalation treatment is much longer in current guidelines; verify.

title: Pneumonia: Communicable Disease View
body:
## What it is
Acute infection that fills the air spaces of one or more lobes with exudate (consolidation). Commonly *Streptococcus pneumoniae*; others in the handout: *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, Friedlander's pneumococcus.

## Must-know facts
- Droplet and fomites; incubation 2-3 days.

## Assessment findings
Rhinitis, chest indrawing, **rusty sputum**, productive cough, high fever, vomiting or convulsions in children, flushed face, chest pain over the lung, dull percussion note over the affected area, concentrated urine.

## Complications
Pleural problems (emphysema/empyema), endocarditis, meningitis, otitis media, jaundice.

## Diagnosis
Chest X-ray, sputum analysis, blood tests.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway and breathing: position for lung expansion, oxygen as ordered, assess respiratory rate and chest indrawing (key sign in children).
2. Frequent turning side to side; bed rest.
3. Adequate fluids, calories, salt, vitamins; tepid sponge bath for fever.
4. Give antibiotics as ordered.

## Prevention
Avoid colds, immunize against pneumococcus and influenza, remove risks (cold, pollution, fatigue, alcohol).

## Related topics
[[Influenza]], [[Tuberculosis: Features and Diagnosis]], [[Measles (Rubeola)]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout lacks treatment drugs and the IMCI classification used in Philippine community programs; add them from your textbook.

title: Tuberculosis: Features and Diagnosis
body:
## What it is
Chronic infection of the lungs by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* (also *M. africanum*, *M. bovis*) forming tubercles that undergo caseation and calcification. The Philippines is among the countries with the highest TB burden.

## Must-know facts
- Airborne, plus direct or indirect contact with sputum, blood from hemoptysis, nasal discharge, saliva.
- Incubation 3-8 weeks (up to 12). Communicable as long as bacilli are in sputum.

## Assessment findings
Cough for **2 weeks or more**, afternoon fever, night sweats, chest or back pain, hemoptysis, weight loss, fatigue, shortness of breath.

## Diagnosis
- **Sputum AFB smear: confirmatory**.
- Chest X-ray.
- Tuberculin tests (Mantoux/PPD, tine, Heaf) show **exposure**, not active disease.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airborne / TB isolation until sputum is negative; cover cough.
2. Ensure sputum collection (early-morning specimen is customary; verify).
3. Start and supervise treatment: see [[Tuberculosis: Treatment and Nursing Care]].
4. Nutrition: high-calorie, small frequent meals; rest periods; stop smoking.

## Prevention and control
BCG for all babies, avoid overcrowding, improve nutrition, tuberculin test for exposed persons, find and treat sources.

## Related topics
[[BCG and Pentavalent Vaccine]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]], [[Pneumonia]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists the tine and Heaf tests, which are rarely used now. Confirm the DOH case-finding rules (symptomatic for 2+ weeks).

title: Tuberculosis: Treatment and Nursing Care
body:
## What it is
Short-course chemotherapy lasts six months with four first-line drugs, taken under **DOTS** (direct observation) to prevent non-adherence and drug resistance.

## Drugs and nursing points
- **Rifampicin**: empty stomach; red-orange body fluids; hepatotoxic and nephrotoxic; permanently stains contact lenses; can make oral contraceptives less effective.
- **Isoniazid (INH)**: empty stomach; peripheral neuropathy (give vitamin B6); avoid alcohol; hepatotoxic.
- **Pyrazinamide**: watch for liver injury (anorexia, fatigue, dark urine), do liver function studies; causes high uric acid.
- **Ethambutol**: food does not matter; report visual changes (optic neuritis); avoid in young children.
- **Streptomycin**: injection; ototoxic, nephrotoxic, neurotoxic; report low urine output.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Observe the client swallowing each dose (DOTS).
2. Teach drug side effects to report: yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, vision change, hearing change, numbness.
3. Teach red-orange urine is expected with rifampicin, not bleeding.
4. Advise women on oral contraceptives to use another method.
5. Maintain respiratory precautions, rest, nutrition, no smoking.

## How the exam asks about it
Match drug to side effect: INH = neuropathy (B6), rifampicin = orange fluids, ethambutol = vision, pyrazinamide = uric acid, streptomycin = hearing and kidney.

## Related topics
[[Tuberculosis: Features and Diagnosis]], [[Treatment of CD, NCD and Emergency Services]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists isoniazid with nephrotoxicity; usually its main toxicities are liver and nerve. Verify dosing timing and the ethambutol age limit.

title: Bird Flu (Avian Influenza)
body:
## What it is
Infectious disease of birds (and less often pigs) from influenza viruses, ranging from mild to severe. Humans can catch the severe strains.

## Must-know facts
- Incubation 3-5 days in humans (per the handout).
- Symptoms: fever, muscle pain, weakness, cough, sore throat, sore eyes, breathing difficulty in severe cases.
- All birds are susceptible; poultry flocks can reach epidemic level fast.

## Control
- Rapid culling, safe disposal of carcasses, quarantine and disinfection of farms.
- Restrict movement of live poultry.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Isolation precautions and strict infection control.
2. Early recognition of cases during poultry outbreaks (ask about poultry contact).
3. Report suspected cases.

## Related topics
[[Influenza]], [[Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS)]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout is brief; add the causative subtype and current DOH reporting rules.

title: Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS)
body:
## What it is
Respiratory illness from a human coronavirus. First known case in China in November 2002; worldwide alert March 2003; first Philippine case April 2003.

## Must-know facts
- Droplet and contact spread.
- Mean incubation 5 days (range 2-10, may reach 14).
- **Prodromal**: fever above 38 C (first sign), chills, malaise, myalgia, headache.
- **Respiratory phase**: dry non-productive cough, hypoxia, crackles, dullness to percussion, decreased breath sounds.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Screen for travel history, symptoms, and close contact.
2. Isolate suspected and probable cases; use barrier nursing with full PPE.
3. Strict handwashing.
4. Monitor oxygenation.

## Related topics
[[Influenza]], [[Bird Flu (Avian Influenza)]], [[Epidemiologic Triangle and Patterns of Disease Occurrence]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout lists "droplet contact" only; confirm precaution level (airborne and contact for aerosol procedures).

title: Cholera
body:
## What it is
Acute bacterial intestinal disease (*Vibrio cholerae* El Tor) with profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting, leading to massive fluid and electrolyte loss, hypovolemic shock, acidosis and death.

## Must-know facts
- Source: vomitus and feces. Spread by food and water contaminated by patients or carriers.
- Incubation 6-48 hours. Infectious during diarrhea and up to about 7 days after.

## Assessment findings
**Rice-water stools**, vomiting, "washerwoman's hands" (wrinkled skin from dehydration), deep rapid breathing (acidosis), low urine output.

## Diagnosis
Rectal swab, stool exam with darkfield microscopy, blood tests (high BUN and creatinine).

## Priority nursing actions
1. **Replace fluid first**: oral rehydration (ORESOL) if able to drink, IV fluids if severe or in shock. Fluid loss kills before the germ does.
2. Monitor vital signs and accurate intake and output.
3. Enteric isolation, handwashing, proper excreta disposal.
4. Antibiotics as ordered (tetracycline and others in the handout).

## Prevention
Protect food and water from feces, boil and chlorinate water, pasteurize milk, sanitary excreta disposal.

## Related topics
[[Typhoid Fever]], [[Bacillary Dysentery (Shigellosis)]], [[Water Supply and Toilet Facilities]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout lists chloramphenicol and furazolidone; current choices differ, and rehydration remains the mainstay.

title: Typhoid Fever
body:
## What it is
Systemic infection by *Salmonella typhi* with prolonged fever and ulceration of Peyer's patches in the intestine.

## Must-know facts
- Fecal-oral; feces and urine are sources; contaminated food, water, milk. Incubation 1-3 weeks. Communicable while bacilli are in excreta (carriers matter).

## Assessment findings
- Onset: headache, nausea/vomiting, **stepladder (ladder-like) fever**, **rose spots** on the abdomen.
- Typhoid state: coma vigil, subsultus tendinum, carphologia, delirium.

## Complications
**Intestinal hemorrhage and perforation** (most dreaded), peritonitis, pneumonia, septicemia, typhoid spine.

## Diagnosis
Typhidot (confirmatory in the handout), ELISA, Widal, stool/rectal swab, bone marrow culture.

## Treatment
Chloramphenicol is called the drug of choice in the handout; alternatives ampicillin, co-trimoxazole, ciprofloxacin, cefixime, azithromycin; ceftriaxone for complicated cases.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Watch for bleeding and perforation: sudden right lower abdominal pain, rigid abdomen, falling BP.
2. Small frequent fluid feedings; monitor vital signs.
3. Enteric precautions; handwashing.
4. Skin and mouth care, turn often.

## Prevention
Excreta disposal, supervise food handlers, safe water, find and treat carriers.

## Related topics
[[Cholera]], [[Bacillary Dysentery (Shigellosis)]], [[Waste, Food Sanitation and Sanitation Laws]]

## Check against your textbook
Heat on the abdomen (handout) conflicts with perforation risk; check. Chloramphenicol is no longer first choice in many places.

title: Bacillary Dysentery (Shigellosis)
body:
## What it is
Acute bacterial intestinal infection (*Shigella* species) with fever, cramps, tenesmus and bloody mucoid stools. Also called bloody flux.

## Must-know facts
- Fecal-oral; contaminated food, water, milk, flies.
- Incubation 12-96 hours (up to a week). Communicable until stool is free of the organism.

## Assessment findings
Fever, tenesmus, nausea/vomiting, headache, colicky pain, anorexia, weakness, bloody-mucoid stool, rapid dehydration.

## Diagnosis
Fresh stool microscopy (mucus, red and white cells), immunofluorescence, sigmoidoscopy (superficial ulcers), stool culture.

## Treatment
Antibiotics (ampicillin, ceftriaxone, co-trimoxazole, ciprofloxacin); IV fluids; low-residue diet. **Antidiarrheals are contraindicated** because they hold the organism in and prolong fever.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Rehydrate and monitor intake and output.
2. Enteric isolation in the acute stage; handwashing.
3. Do not give antidiarrheals.

## Prevention
Sanitary stool disposal, handwashing after defecation, food hygiene, fly control, safe water.

## Related topics
[[Amoebiasis]], [[Cholera]], [[Typhoid Fever]]

title: Amoebiasis
body:
## What it is
Protozoal infection by *Entamoeba histolytica* that begins in the colon and can spread to liver and lungs.

## Must-know facts
- **Cyst** = infective stage and hardy outside the body; **trophozoite** = invasive form.
- Fecal-oral; contaminated food, water, flies. Average incubation 2-4 weeks. Communicable while cysts are in stool.

## Assessment findings
- Acute: diarrhea alternating with constipation, foul watery stool with blood-streaked mucus, lower abdominal gas, right iliac tenderness.
- Chronic: weeks of diarrhea then constipation, weight loss, weakness, bloody mucoid stools.

## Diagnosis
Stool exam for cysts; leukocytosis; sigmoidoscopy for ulcers.

## Treatment
Metronidazole (Flagyl) is the main drug; others listed in the handout are tetracycline, ampicillin, streptomycin, chloramphenicol.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Enteric precautions.
2. Stool specimen: no oil preparations for 48 hours beforehand, choose portion with blood and mucus, label, send immediately (live trophozoites die when cooled).
3. Keep warm, force fluids, bland low-residue diet.
4. Skin care.

## Prevention
Fly control, safe water, food handling, treat carriers, sanitary excreta disposal.

## Related topics
[[Bacillary Dysentery (Shigellosis)]], [[Water Supply and Toilet Facilities]], [[Trichomoniasis]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's metronidazole dose (800 mg TID x 5 days) should be verified; do not memorize it without checking.

title: Paragonimiasis (Lung Fluke)
body:
## What it is
Lung fluke infection (*Paragonimus westermani*) acquired by eating raw or undercooked crabs and crayfish. Reservoir hosts: cats, dogs, rats, pigs.

## Assessment findings
Long-lasting cough, recurrent blood-streaked sputum, chest and back pain. **Looks like TB but does not respond to anti-TB drugs.**

## Diagnosis and treatment
Sputum microscopy, immunologic tests; cerebral involvement possible. Drug: praziquantel.

## Priority nursing actions
- Teach to cook crabs and crayfish thoroughly.
- Treat infected people; health education; control snail hosts.

## How the exam asks about it
TB-like symptoms plus raw crab eating, or poor response to TB therapy.

## Related topics
[[Tuberculosis: Features and Diagnosis]], [[Schistosomiasis]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]]

title: Mumps
body:
## What it is
Acute viral disease (paramyxovirus) causing swelling of one or both parotid glands, sometimes testes and other glands.

## Must-know facts
- Spread by direct contact and articles soiled with nose/throat secretions.
- Communicable from up to a week before swelling to 9 days after; **highest in the 48 hours before swelling**.

## Assessment findings
Sudden headache, earache, anorexia, fever, parotid swelling between earlobe and jaw angle.

## Complications
**Orchitis** (can threaten fertility), oophoritis, mastitis, meningoencephalitis, pancreatitis, deafness, myocarditis, nephritis.

## Diagnosis
Serum amylase (early clue), complement fixation, hemagglutination inhibition, viral culture.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Isolation (single room, droplet).
2. Pain and fever: analgesics, antipyretics, warm or cold compresses.
3. Oral care with warm salt-water gargles; soft bland diet; **avoid acid foods and juices** that provoke pain.
4. Extra fluids, bed rest, report cases.

## Prevention
MMR vaccine.

## Related topics
[[Measles (Rubeola)]], [[German Measles (Rubella)]], [[Expanded Program on Immunization]]

title: Botulism
body:
## What it is
Severe poisoning by a neurotoxin of *Clostridium botulinum* (gram-positive anaerobe) causing **descending flaccid paralysis**. Forms: foodborne, wound, infant.

## Must-know facts
- Sources: improperly canned low-acid or home-canned foods, cured meats, smoked fish, honey and corn syrup (infants). Spores survive boiling for hours.
- Incubation 12-72 hours (range 2 hours to 10 days).

## Assessment findings
Double or blurred vision, drooping eyelids, dry mouth, trouble swallowing, speaking and breathing, descending weakness, reduced reflexes, early vomiting/diarrhea then constipation.

## Diagnosis
Toxin in serum or stool, food culture, mouse test (most direct), EMG; rule out myasthenia gravis and Guillain-Barre.

## Priority nursing actions
1. **Airway and breathing**: monitor respiratory function; ventilation may be needed.
2. Give botulinum antitoxin after allergy history and skin test.
3. Frequent neurologic checks; NG feeding if swallowing is impaired; purge GI tract as ordered.
4. Food history; notify authorities and identify others exposed.

## Teaching
Cook food thoroughly, boil home-canned food 10 minutes, no honey for infants (verify), treat wounds promptly, avoid street injectables.

## Related topics
[[Tetanus (Lockjaw) Disease]], [[Anthrax]], [[Poliomyelitis]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout suggests inducing vomiting in infants; this is not standard. Confirm.

title: Schistosomiasis
body:
## What it is
Blood fluke disease (snail fever). In the Philippines: ***Schistosoma japonicum***; intermediate host is the snail ***Oncomelania hupensis quadrasi***. Endemic areas include Leyte and Samar.

## Must-know facts
- Spread through contact with contaminated water; larvae (cercariae) penetrate skin. Source: stool and urine of infected people and animals.
- Incubation at least 2 months.

## Stages
1. **Swimmer's itch** 24 hours after skin penetration.
2. Bloody mucoid stool and **Katayama fever** (fever, headache, cough, chills, lymph node and liver/spleen enlargement).
3. Chronic: egg granulomas in intestine, liver, bladder; jaundice, ascites, big spleen, brain involvement (seizures), hematuria.

## Complications
Cirrhosis, portal hypertension, esophageal varices, ascites, bladder cancer, heart and renal failure.

## Diagnosis
Stool exam, biopsy, ELISA, **circumoval precipitin test (COPT) confirmatory**.

## Treatment
Praziquantel (drug of choice).

## Priority nursing actions
Comfort, skin care, nutrition, tepid sponge bath; monitor for bleeding and liver failure.

## Prevention
Kill snails (molluscicides, clear vegetation), sanitary excreta disposal, control stray animals, safe water, footbridges over snail streams, health education.

## Related topics
[[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Filariasis]], [[Paragonimiasis (Lung Fluke)]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's 6-month praziquantel schedule is doubtful (usually a one-day course). Verify.

title: Syphilis
body:
## What it is
Sexually transmitted infection by the spirochete *Treponema pallidum*. Also transmitted by contact with lesions or blood, and across the placenta.

## Stages
- **Primary**: painless chancre at entry site, swollen glands; heals in 3-6 weeks without treatment (the disease is not gone).
- **Secondary**: rash (macular, papular, pustular) including palms and soles, temporary hair loss, brittle pitted nails.
- **Latent**: no symptoms, dormant.
- **Late**: damage to brain, heart, liver and other organs.

## Diagnosis
Darkfield test of lesion (immediate), VDRL (nonspecific, reactive about 1-2 weeks after chancre), FTA-ABS, CSF protein above 40 mg/dL for neurosyphilis.

## Treatment
IM benzathine penicillin G; tetracycline or doxycycline for those allergic.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Finish the whole treatment even if symptoms disappear.
2. Standard precautions; keep secondary lesions dry.
3. Trace and treat partners; report to DOH.
4. Sex education.

## Related topics
[[Gonorrhea]], [[Chlamydia]], [[HIV/AIDS: Diagnosis and Nursing Care]]

title: Trichomoniasis
body:
## What it is
STI from the protozoan *Trichomonas vaginalis*. Direct sexual contact or sharing damp items (towels, douching equipment). Incubation 5-21 days.

## Assessment findings
- Women: white or greenish-yellow foul discharge, vaginal itching and soreness, painful urination.
- Men: mild penile itching, painful urination, clear discharge (often few symptoms).

## Diagnosis
Microscopy of discharge, culture, rapid test (10-45 minutes, less accurate).

## Treatment
**Metronidazole** (Flagyl) is the treatment of choice; tinidazole is an alternative. Treat partners.

## Priority nursing actions
- Standard precautions; help with specimen collection.
- **No alcohol** during metronidazole and for 48 hours after (nausea, vomiting, flushing, headache).

## Complication
Cervical cancer (as listed in the handout).

## Related topics
[[Candidiasis]], [[Chlamydia]], [[Gonorrhea]]

## Check against your textbook
Link to cervical cancer is weak in current evidence; verify.

title: Chlamydia
body:
## What it is
STI by *Chlamydia trachomatis*, spread by vaginal or rectal intercourse and oral-genital contact. Incubation 7-14 days; infectious until treated.

## Assessment findings
Cervical erosion, mucopurulent discharge, painful intercourse, abdominal pain, fever, urinary burning and frequency, painful scrotal swelling.

## Complications
Sterility, prematurity, stillbirth, infant pneumonia and eye infection.

## Diagnosis and treatment
Culture, nucleic acid probe. Tetracycline, erythromycin or azithromycin.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Complete full antibiotic course.
2. Notify and treat partners; offer HIV testing for both.
3. Assess newborns of infected mothers.
4. Hygiene: avoid touching discharge, wash hands before touching eyes.

## Related topics
[[Gonorrhea]], [[Syphilis]], [[HIV/AIDS: Diagnosis and Nursing Care]]

title: Gonorrhea
body:
## What it is
STI by *Neisseria gonorrhoeae* affecting the genitourinary tract, rectum and throat. Incubation 2-5 days. Passed through intercourse, contaminated secretions in vaginal delivery, and fomites.

## Assessment findings
- Women: about 80% **asymptomatic**; burning and frequency, yellowish purulent discharge.
- Men: painful urination with purulent discharge, urethritis, prostatitis.

## Complications
Sterility, pelvic infection, epididymitis, arthritis, endocarditis, conjunctivitis (newborn), meningitis.

## Diagnosis and treatment
Gram stain, culture. Ceftriaxone IM; azithromycin or doxycycline by mouth.

## Priority nursing actions
- Standard precautions; abstain from sex until cured; treat partners.
- Moist heat for gonococcal arthritis.
- Sex education, case finding, reporting.

## Related topics
[[Chlamydia]], [[Syphilis]], [[Newborn Screening]]

title: Candidiasis
body:
## What it is
Superficial fungal infection by *Candida albicans*, part of normal flora that overgrows when glucose is high or immunity is low.

## Assessment findings by site
- Skin: scaly red rash in folds (under breasts, axillae, groin).
- Nails: red swollen nail bed.
- Mouth (**thrush**): creamy white curd-like patches that bleed when scraped.
- Esophagus: painful swallowing.
- Vagina: white or yellow discharge with itching.
- Deep spread: lungs, kidney, brain, heart, eye.

## Diagnosis and treatment
Blood or vaginal culture; echocardiography if heart involved. Antifungals: nystatin, clotrimazole, miconazole.

## Priority nursing actions
Oral care, control blood sugar, keep skin folds dry, teach correct antifungal use.

## Related topics
[[Trichomoniasis]], [[HIV/AIDS: Diagnosis and Nursing Care]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout's text is cut after antifungals; add management details from a textbook.

title: HIV/AIDS: Diagnosis and Nursing Care
body:
## What it is
Infection that destroys immune defenses. The part of the handout covering the cause, transmission and symptoms is missing from the extracted text; this note covers what survives.

## Diagnosis
- **ELISA**: presumptive (screening).
- **Western blot**: confirmatory.
- Particle agglutination and immunofluorescence also listed.

## Treatment
Antiretrovirals: reverse transcriptase inhibitors (zidovudine), protease inhibitors (ritonavir).

## Priority nursing actions (protect the health worker)
1. Standard precautions: gloves for blood specimens, handwashing, no contact with open skin lesions.
2. Do not bend needles; discard in puncture-resistant containers.
3. Label blood and specimens prominently.
4. Sterilize lensed instruments; clean thermometers with warm soapy water then soak in 70% alcohol 10 minutes.
5. Isolate clients with active AIDS to protect them from infection (reverse isolation concept).

## Related topics
[[Syphilis]], [[Candidiasis]], [[Isolation Categories and Precautions]]

## Check against your textbook
Missing: causative virus, modes of transmission, clinical stages, opportunistic infections, counseling, Philippine HIV law. Add them. Isolating AIDS clients is for their protection, not because they are a hazard.

title: Dengue Fever
body:
## What it is
Acute febrile viral disease from dengue virus types 1-4, spread by the day-biting female *Aedes aegypti* mosquito. No person-to-person spread; people are infectious to mosquitoes while febrile. Incubation 3-15 days.

## Assessment findings
Herman's sign (rash with islands of normal skin) is called pathognomonic.
1. **Febrile**: first ~4 days, high fever 39-40 C, pain, headache.
2. **Toxic/hemorrhagic (critical)**: temperature **falls**, severe abdominal pain, vomiting, melena, hematemesis. Falling fever with shock signs is the danger.
3. **Convalescent**: flushing with white patches, stable BP.

## Diagnosis
Tourniquet (Rumpel-Leede) test, low platelets, hemoconcentration (hematocrit up 20% or more), occult blood, NS1 test.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Watch for shock and bleeding (circulation).
2. Rapid fluid replacement; oral rehydration; oxygen; transfusion for severe bleeding.
3. Paracetamol for fever, **no aspirin** (bleeding).
4. Nosebleed: ice bag to forehead and nasal bridge.
5. Nursing diet: low fat, low fiber, non-irritating, no carbonated drinks.
6. Keep patient under a mosquito net.

## Prevention
Remove breeding sites, treated nets, early case detection and treatment, health education (clean up, cover water containers).

## Related topics
[[Malaria]], [[Filariasis]], [[Environmental Sanitation]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout bundles chikungunya and other names; verify.

title: Malaria
body:
## What it is
Parasitic disease by *Plasmodium* (falciparum most common, vivax, malariae, ovale), transmitted by the bite of the female **Anopheles** mosquito; also by transfusion and across the placenta. Endemic example: Palawan.

## Incubation
falciparum 5-7 days; vivax 6-8; ovale 8-9; malariae 12-16.

## Assessment findings
Paroxysms with shaking chills, rapidly rising fever and severe headache, then profuse sweating; muscle pain, enlarged spleen and liver.

## Prevention and control
- Chloroquine weekly, starting 1-2 weeks before entering an endemic area.
- Treated mosquito nets, house spraying, stream clearing and seeding, long clothing in evening, avoid outdoor night activity (9 PM-3 AM), neem trees, zooprophylaxis.

## Priority nursing actions
Protect from bites, give antimalarials as ordered, manage fever and chills, monitor for complications, report cases.

## Related topics
[[Dengue Fever]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]], [[Filariasis]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout has no treatment section or diagnosis (blood smear). Add them.

title: Filariasis
body:
## What it is
Parasitic disease from thread-like filarial worms (*Wuchereria bancrofti*, *Brugia malayi*) spread by mosquito (*Aedes poecilus* in the handout). Disabling and stigmatizing. Incubation 8-16 months. Endemic example: Sorsogon.

## Stages
- Asymptomatic.
- Acute: lymphadenitis, lymphangitis, epididymitis, orchitis.
- Chronic (10-15 years later): hydrocele, lymphedema, **elephantiasis**.

## Diagnosis
Nocturnal blood examination (blood drawn around 8 PM because microfilariae circulate at night). Immunochromatographic test (ICT) is a rapid antigen test done in daytime.

## Treatment and prevention
Diethylcarbamazine citrate (Hetrazan); yearly mass drug dose; nets and repellents.

## Priority nursing actions
Health education, sanitation, hygiene of affected limbs, psychological support for body image.

## Related topics
[[Malaria]], [[Dengue Fever]], [[Locally Endemic Diseases]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout confusingly mentions "African eye worm" (Loa loa) and a vector name; verify.

title: Leptospirosis
body:
## What it is
Bacterial zoonosis by *Leptospira interrogans*. Animal urine (rats, dogs, pigs) contaminates floodwater or food; bacteria enter through **skin wounds** or mucous membranes. Incubation 7-13 days.

## Assessment findings
- **Leptospiremic** (4-7 days): fever, headache, muscle pain (calf), vomiting.
- **Immune** (4-30 days): meningeal irritation, little or no urine, severe cases shock and heart failure.
- Convalescence: relapse possible week 4-5.

## Complications
Meningitis, respiratory distress, kidney tubular necrosis, heart problems.

## Treatment
Penicillin, doxycycline (also prophylaxis), tetracycline, erythromycin; fluids, electrolytes, blood.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Monitor urine output (kidney failure) and breathing.
2. Skin care; darkened room; oral fluids.
3. Teach: avoid wading in flood water, wear boots, rat control, drainage.

## Related topics
[[Environmental Sanitation]], [[Rabies]], [[Anthrax]]

## Check against your textbook
Handout lists "isolate patient"; standard precautions are usual. Doxycycline prophylaxis is typically given after flood exposure per DOH advisory; verify.

title: Rabies
body:
## What it is
Fatal viral infection (rhabdovirus) passed through saliva of an infected animal, usually a bite. Incubation 3-8 weeks (9 days to 7 years); shorter with deep bites near the head.

## Phases
- **Prodromal**: fever, malaise, irritability, light and sound sensitivity.
- **Excitement**: hydrophobia, aerophobia, painful throat spasms, drooling.
- **Paralytic**: quiet, unconscious, paralysis, respiratory and heart failure.

## Diagnosis
Fluorescent rabies antibody (most definitive); Negri bodies in animal brain.

## Priority nursing actions
1. **Wash the wound immediately** with soap and running water, then apply antiseptic (povidone iodine). This is the first priority.
2. Refer for anti-rabies vaccine and immune globulin.
3. In hospital: quiet room, no running water in view, concurrent and terminal disinfection; protect staff from saliva.

## Prevention
Vaccinate dogs at 3 months and yearly; confine a biting dog 10-14 days for observation; public education.

## Related topics
[[Tetanus (Lockjaw) Disease]], [[Leptospirosis]]

## Check against your textbook
The handout says "patients should not be bathed"; verify and check Philippine Rabies Act details.

title: Tetanus (Lockjaw) Disease
body:
## What it is
Illness from the toxin of *Clostridium tetani*. Spores from soil and feces enter through dirty wounds, injection drug use, or sometimes surgery. Incubation 3-21 days.

## Assessment findings
Localized: spasm near the wound. Generalized: **trismus (lockjaw)**, risus sardonicus, neck stiffness, arched back (opisthotonos), board-like abdomen, spasms with sensory stimuli, sweating, fast heart rate. Death from airway spasm.

## Treatment
Wound care, metronidazole (first line) or penicillin G, **tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG)**, sedatives and muscle relaxants, intubation if needed, treat autonomic instability.

## Priority nursing actions
1. Airway and ventilation, suction, watch respiratory distress.
2. **Quiet, dim room**; minimal stimulation.
3. IV line, cardiac monitoring, accurate intake and output.
4. Nutrition for high metabolic demand; passive range of motion.
5. Teach wound care and booster every 10 years.

## Related topics
[[Tetanus Toxoid Immunization]], [[Botulism]], [[Pertussis (Whooping Cough)]]

title: Poliomyelitis
body:
## What it is
Viral disease (poliovirus 1, 2, 3) spread by oropharyngeal secretions or feces. Incubation 7-14 days.

## Assessment findings
Fever, headache, vomiting, neck, back and limb pain, muscle tenderness and weakness, loss of reflexes, positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs, **tripod sign**, Hoyne sign, urinary retention, difficulty swallowing.

## Diagnosis
Stool culture, rising antibody titer, CSF changes, EMG.

## Treatment and nursing
- Analgesics (no morphine per handout), moist heat, bed rest until pain eases, physical therapy, braces.
- **Airway and breathing first**: watch for respiratory failure; check BP.
- Skin care, reposition, balanced diet, handwashing.

## Complications
Respiratory failure, pulmonary edema, pneumonia, urinary tract infection, cor pulmonale.

## Prevention
Oral polio vaccine; boosters before travel to endemic areas.

## Related topics
[[Expanded Program on Immunization]], [[Vaccine Principles and Nursing Responsibilities]], [[Botulism]]

## Check against your textbook
Current schedules also use inactivated polio vaccine; verify.
